1018. ἀμαρυγάς: the, as it were, continuous movements. And in the case of fire, “to flash” (ἀμαρύσσειν) is said from the flame darting continuously. Homer (θ 265): “he gazed at the twinkling of their feet,” meaning the motion that cannot be grasped.

1019–21. τηκομένη οἷόν τε: he paraphrased the Homeric passage (Ψ 598 sq.): “and he warmed as when dew upon ears of a growing crop.” Now what melts certainly also warms (μ 175 sq.): “and quickly the wax warmed, since the great strength of the sun commanded it.” But not everything that warms also melts. Hence Homer, having said “warmed,” added “as when” speaking metaphorically, so that the meaning is expressive of the pleasure of the ears of grain as if they were alive, the dew clinging to the fruits when they hold their stalk upright, as if raised aloft; so too the soul of Menelaus was moved to delight by the words of Antilochus. But to compare the delighted soul to melting is not plausible.
It is possible, then, to read τηκομένη also in the sense of delight. For what melts, when it is loosened, certainly also becomes soft. So one can say that Medea was wholly dissolved, spread out.
